41.text: I finally passed my driving test on the fourth try. My instructor clapped. I cried a little in the parking lot and then drove us both home.
Kept my sourdough starter alive for eleven months now. It has outlived three houseplants and one relationship.
I read forty pages of a novel in Spanish without touching the dictionary. Ten years ago I couldn't order coffee.
We paid off the last of the hospital bills in March. Nobody threw a party, but I sat in the car and let out a breath I'd been holding for two years.
Made the volleyball team as libero after getting cut last year. Coach still yells at me, but now it's the good kind of yelling.
At seventy-three I learned to video call without holding the phone to my ear. My grandchildren no longer talk to my ceiling.
I quit a job everyone said was a dream job. Sleeping through the night again feels like an achievement worth listing somewhere.
Grew tomatoes on a Berlin balcony that gets four hours of sun a day. Harvested nine of them. Nine!
My daughter and I ran the 5k together and she waited for me at every kilometer marker. Proud of finishing, prouder of how I raised her.
Stood up at a town meeting and spoke against the road widening. My voice shook the whole time, but I said every word I'd planned.
I filed my own taxes in a country whose language I've spoken for only two years. The clerk stamped it and said nothing. Silence means perfect.
Went a full year without buying new clothes. Mended things instead. My grandmother's thimble finally got used for something.
I taught my father to swim at sixty-one. He gripped the pool edge for three whole weekends before he let go. Then he let go.
Defended my thesis in a blazer I bought secondhand that morning. Four years of work, twenty minutes of questions, one very long nap after.
Finally said no to hosting the holidays this year. The world did not end. My sister even sounded relieved.
I stayed. That's all. There were months this year when leaving everything felt easier, and I stayed, and it's getting lighter.

43.text: Congee with century egg, from my grandmother, who made it whenever I was sick. Now I make it when I'm homesick, which is a kind of sick too.
Buttered toast dipped in milky tea. My grandfather called it a workman's breakfast and shared his with me before school.
Instant ramen with an egg cracked in, perfected at 2am with my university roommate. We called it exam soup.
My mother's dal with too much ghee. She says the ghee is the point and that cardiologists simply lack imagination.
Pierogi with fried onions. My aunt taught me to pinch the edges, warning that sloppy pierogi mean a sloppy heart. I still hear her at the stove.
Arroz con leche with cinnamon on top, from the neighbor who watched us after school. Hers was better than my mother's and we all knew it.
Marmite on thick toast. My dad ate it, so five-year-old me insisted on it too. Everyone else in the house thinks we're broken.
Cold watermelon with salt, eaten on the porch in August. My grandfather swore the salt was scientific. Really it's his voice I'm tasting.
Miso soup with extra tofu. A host mother in Osaka made it every morning of my exchange year, and now no other breakfast feels honest.
Boxed macaroni with ketchup, courtesy of my older brother on nights our parents worked late. Fancy versions exist. They're wrong.
Chicken soup with lemon squeezed in, the way my mother-in-law taught me. She handed over the recipe like she was handing me the family.
Plain rice with a fried egg and soy sauce. Nobody introduced me; being broke did. I could afford anything now and I still choose it.
Jollof rice from the bottom of the pot, the crispy part. My cousins and I fought over it every Sunday until our grandmother made a rota.
Bread with condensed milk. My grandmother kept a tin in the cupboard for after chores, and the sound of it opening still means rest.
Pho at six in the morning from the stall near my childhood house. My father took me before school and we never talked, just slurped. It was enough.
Mashed potatoes with a lake of gravy in the middle. My grandad engineered the lake personally. He took the technique very seriously.

45.text: The noise level. Six conversations, a kettle, someone's bad singing. My apartment is so quiet now that I leave the radio on for company.
Hearing my dad's laugh through a wall instead of through a speaker. Phones flatten it. In person it made the cupboards rattle.
Someone always stole my fries and I complained every single time. Nobody steals my fries anymore and honestly they taste worse now.
Being able to hug my mother without booking a flight first. With a nine-hour time difference, even our phone calls need a calendar.
Playing cards past midnight while the uncles argued over rules nobody ever wrote down. The arguing was the game, really.
I miss having witnesses. People who saw the small stuff, the burnt dinners, the bad haircuts. Now every story needs a preamble.
The queue for the one bathroom. Never thought I'd say that. You learn a lot about people from who bangs on a door at 7am and how.
My grandmother deciding everyone was too thin and cooking accordingly. Being fussed over is a luxury I didn't recognize until customs stamps.
Sunday lunch stretching into dinner because nobody wanted to be the first to leave. Now goodbyes happen when a battery runs out.
The way plans got made by shouting up the stairs. Now organizing one dinner takes a group chat, three polls, and a spreadsheet.
Sharing weather. Sounds silly, but when it rained, it rained on all of us. Now I check three forecasts just to imagine everyone's day.
My little brother falling asleep on my shoulder during movies. He's taller than me now and lives in another hemisphere.
Grieving together. When our grandfather died, those of us abroad mourned alone by phone. Sorrow needs a full room and shared bad coffee.
Leftovers. A full house makes leftovers, and leftovers make Mondays bearable. Cooking for one produces nothing worth reheating.
Being interrupted. Everyone talking over everyone, finishing each other's stories wrong on purpose. Video calls are so polite it hurts.
The pile of shoes at the door. You could read the whole evening from it, who was home, who brought a friend, who left in a hurry.

47.text: Singing. Not concert singing, just birthday-party singing that doesn't make my nephew cover his ears in front of the cake.
I wish I could draw the faces I remember. My grandmother's is getting blurry, and there isn't a single good photo of her laughing.
Whistling with two fingers. My grandfather could summon dogs, children, and taxis with one blast. The secret went with him.
Falling asleep anywhere, like my husband can. Planes, waiting rooms, weddings. I lie awake cataloguing regrets; he snores through turbulence.
Perfect pitch. My daughter hears a note and names it like she's reading a street sign. I want to know what the world sounds like to her.
Making small talk that doesn't sound like a job interview. Some people simply chat with strangers. I prepare questions in advance.
I'd like to dance without counting. At every wedding I do maths with my feet while my cousins just move like water.
Fixing engines. My father could hear a problem before he opened the hood. I pay a man to plug my car into a laptop.
Languages. My grandmother spoke four and could use all of them in one scolding. I got two, and one is mostly kitchen vocabulary now.
Baking bread that actually rises. Mine come out like commemorative bricks. My sister claims the yeast can sense fear.
Telling stories the way old fishermen do, slowly, with pauses that make you lean in. I rush every punchline like I'm charged by the second.
Sitting still. Real stillness, like the old men outside the tea house who watch a whole afternoon go by and call it a good day.
Remembering birthdays without an app. My mother holds about ninety of them in her head, along with everyone's exam dates.
Calligraphy. My grandfather's brush strokes hung in our hallway for forty years. My handwriting looks like a heart monitor readout.
Swimming properly. I grew up an hour from the sea and can only manage a panicked frog paddle. My kids are dolphins and show no mercy.
Comforting people. Some know exactly what to say at a hospital bedside. I fold blankets and refill water glasses and hope it counts.

49.text: My son comes home from his semester abroad on the 14th. I've already planned three dinners and I'm pretending I haven't.
First frost. I know that's an odd answer, but the garden finally gets to rest, and so, by long tradition, do I.
The mango crate from my uncle's farm arrives this month. We eat them over the sink like animals and discuss nothing else for days.
My granddaughter's first school play. She's a tree with one line and I will be filming it like it's the moon landing.
Payday lands before rent for once. Small thing, but this month I get to buy groceries without doing arithmetic in the aisle.
We're scattering my mother's ashes at the lake she swam in as a girl. Not a happy thing, but I'm looking forward to it being done gently.
The library's reading challenge ends and I'm two books from beating the man who always wins. He doesn't know we're competing.
The monsoon is supposed to break this month. The first evening it rains, the whole street comes out and just stands in it.
My best friend and I have a standing call on the first Sunday of every month, three time zones apart. Twenty-two years running.
Exams end on the 19th and I have planned exactly nothing afterward. The nothing is the point. A whole afternoon of legal nothing.
The night market opens back up by the river. I go for the grilled squid and stay for the aunties gossiping at the next stall.
My cast comes off. I will never again take putting on a sock for granted, and I have promised my left arm a long apology.
We find out the baby's due date this month. My wife wants a spring child, I want a healthy one, and my mother wants twins for some reason.
There's a night this month when the power company has scheduled an outage. The village will sit outside and the stars will be ridiculous.
My brother and I are repainting our parents' fence like we did as kids, except this time nobody is being paid in ice cream. Sadly.
Nothing large. But the jacaranda at the corner should bloom, and I time my walks to it every year. Purple for two weeks, then gone.

51.text: A worn dictionary from my father when I left for university. Inside, he'd underlined the word 'begin' and nothing else.
My grandmother's sewing machine, still smelling of machine oil. It came with her handwritten notes tucked under the plate.
A drawing of our old dog from my daughter, done from memory two years after he died. She got the crooked ear exactly right.
When I was ten, a bicycle bell. Not a bicycle, just the bell, from my uncle, with a promise attached. The bike came a year later. He kept score.
A plane ticket home, bought quietly by my coworkers when my mother fell ill. I found it in an envelope on my desk with no card.
The bottom bunk. My big sister gave it up for a whole year when I broke my leg, and to an eight-year-old that was the crown jewels.
A cassette my late husband made of himself reading my favorite poems, badly, laughing halfway through most of them. Best thing I own.
My father's watch, given the night before my first job. It runs six minutes fast because he always was, and I've never corrected it.
Socks, honestly. Hand-knitted by a neighbor the winter our heating failed. Wool has never meant so much before or since.
For my fiftieth, my kids paid off a debt I never told them about. I still don't know how they found out. We don't discuss it. I cried in the garage.
An empty notebook from my high school teacher with 'you have things to say' on the first page. I've bought the same brand for thirty years.
A jar of soil from our old village, carried through two airports by my cousin. It sits by my window in Toronto and outweighs everything I own.
My grandfather taught me chess as my tenth birthday present. No box, no bow, no wrapping. Forty years on, it's still the gift I use most.
The year we had nothing, my mother wrapped up her own bracelet for me. I only understood what that actually was much, much later.
A goat. My whole class chipped in and donated a goat in my name to a farm charity. I have never laughed harder at a certificate.
Noise-cancelling headphones from my teenagers, with a note that said 'so you can't hear us'. Self-aware and genuinely useful.

53.text: It smells like rice about to finish cooking. Someone is always half-asleep on the sofa. The door sticks, and we all know the exact hip-check that opens it.
Home is wherever my wife puts the blue teapot. We've moved eight times across four countries. The teapot has never broken, so neither have we.
It's the one place I don't rehearse before speaking. My accent relaxes there. Even my shoulders know the address.
Two dogs at the gate, always announcing me like news. A mango tree my father planted the year I was born. Power cuts nobody complains about anymore.
Home is a phone number I've known since I was five. It still rings in the same hallway. My mother still answers before the second ring.
It's not the house, because we sold the house. It's my sister doing the crossword out loud. It follows her from apartment to apartment.
The floor is always slightly gritty with beach sand. The freezer holds more fish than ice. You can hear the sea whenever the fridge stops humming.
Home is a language I only speak with four other people. It has its own jokes and no dictionary. When we're together, I'm fluent again.
Winter boots drying by the radiator. My grandmother's icon in the corner, watching everything. Tea strong enough to stand a spoon in.
It's the smell of diesel and frying garlic from the street below. Laundry lines cross between buildings like handwriting. My city, seventh floor, third window.
Home used to be a place. Then it became my husband's snoring. I complain about it daily and can no longer sleep in a silent room.
The clock my grandfather wound every Sunday still ticks there. Nobody else winds it quite right. Time literally runs differently in that house.
It's a group chat that never sleeps. Photos of dinner arrive from three continents. Someone is always awake and someone is always cooking.
Home is my mother telling me to eat before asking how I am. It's slippers appearing at my feet before I've shut the door. It's never having to knock.
A creaky third stair I still skip out of habit. A pencil line on the kitchen door frame for every age I've been. Rooms that got smaller as I grew.
For now, a rented room and one good frying pan. But I burn the same brand of incense my parents use. Same smoke, six thousand kilometers apart.

55.text: Octopuses have three hearts, and two of them stop when they swim. My grandson told me at dinner and I've been thinking about it all week.
My quiet father was a champion ballroom dancer in the sixties. I found the medals in a biscuit tin while helping him move. He just shrugged.
Bananas are berries and strawberries aren't. My daughter announced this like a lawyer, and now every dinner has a fact-check segment.
I learned that rest is a skill you can be bad at. Sat down to do nothing for one hour and lasted eleven minutes. Training continues.
Honey found in Egyptian tombs is still edible after three thousand years. I keep looking at the jar in my pantry with new respect.
That my grandmother crossed a border on foot at nineteen, alone. Seventy years of Sunday lunches and she only mentioned it last month.
Turns out the moon is slowly leaving us, a few centimeters a year. Everything drifts, even the moon. I don't know why that comforted me.
My teenage son can cook. Properly, with seasoning. Fifteen years of chicken nugget demands, and apparently he was studying me the whole time.
Our surname was changed at an immigration desk in 1952 because the officer couldn't spell it. One tired stranger renamed us all.
Cows have best friends and get anxious when they're separated. I grew up on a dairy farm and somehow nobody ever said it out loud.
The wiring in our house was done by my mother, not my father, back in 1974. She let everyone assume otherwise for fifty years. Legendary restraint.
I learned my knees have an expiry date the hard way, playing football with my nephews. The mind writes checks the cartilage can't cash.
Apparently I talk in my sleep, in my first language, which I barely use anymore. My roommate learned to say good morning in it, just to reply.
The pyramids were as ancient to Cleopatra as she is to us. My history teacher dropped that on a Tuesday and I stared at the wall for a while.
Sea otters hold hands while sleeping so they don't drift apart. My five-year-old now insists we do the same at nap time. I comply.
I learned that declining a second helping at my aunt's table is technically possible. Nobody was harmed. Physics held. She still texted my mother.

57.text: The village in Sicily my great-grandparents left in 1908. I want us all standing in the square they last saw, eating too much, staying too long.
Lapland in deep winter, all of us in one glass cabin under the aurora. The kids can hunt for reindeer; I'll hunt for silence.
A sleeper train across the whole country, no destination, the family filling three compartments. The journey is the place.
Back to the lake house we rented once in 1999 and never managed again. Same week, same cousins, hopefully the same terrible rowboat.
The Galapagos, so my mother can finally see the tortoises she's been reading about for forty years. Everyone else is welcome to tag along.
A tiny island in the Philippines where my grandmother grew up. She hasn't been back since the war. I would carry her onto the boat myself.
Japan in cherry blossom season, all sixteen of us on a bullet train with too much luggage, my father pretending he isn't crying at the flowers.
A safari, but the slow kind where you sit still for hours. I want my city grandchildren to hear a lion before they see one.
Honestly? A whole floor of a Tokyo arcade for a weekend. My grandmother included. She has undiagnosed rhythm-game talent; I've seen it at weddings.
The fjords, on a boat big enough that nobody has to share a bathroom. Family harmony has architectural requirements.
Machu Picchu, but we take the long trail up so my brother can't check his phone for four days. That's the real destination.
One month renting the old family farm back from its new owners. Money can't buy much of the past, but it could buy that.
Antarctica. I want the whole family to find out what quiet actually is, and penguins are famously excellent with children.
Mecca, together, while my parents are still strong enough to walk it. We've talked about it every Ramadan since I was small.
A campsite, honestly, any campsite, but with everyone's flights paid so nobody has an excuse. The luxury isn't the place, it's full attendance.
New Zealand in a slow convoy of camper vans. My sister drives ahead, we argue by radio, and we stop wherever the sheep look photogenic.

59.text: 'What was your mother like as a person, not a mother?' I've been assembling the answer for years and nobody has ever requested it.
'Are you tired?' Not as a greeting, but really asking. I'd say yes, since 2021, and it would be such a relief just to say it out loud.
'What did you want to be before you got practical?' A marine biologist. I still watch the documentaries and mouth the fish names.
'How did you two actually meet?' Everyone knows the wedding version. The true version involves a stolen umbrella and I'm ready to confess.
'What do you do all day?' I'm retired, and people stopped asking. I birdwatch, I repair clocks, I have opinions. Ask me about the clocks.
I wish my kids would ask how I'm finding this stage of parenting, the way I ask about their lives. Answer: winging it, terrified, loving it.
'What's the dish you can't make like she did?' My grandmother's flatbread. I have the recipe, the pan, her rolling pin. It's not the same, and I know why.
'What are you reading?' Simple, but it opens every door I actually want opened. Currently a history of lighthouses, and yes, I'll gladly elaborate.
'When did you feel bravest?' The night bus to a city where I knew nobody, age twenty-two, one suitcase. Nobody asks, so I tell myself.
'Do you want help, or do you want listening?' My daughter asked me that once and it rearranged something in me. I wish it would catch on.
'What was your favorite year?' 1987. I won't explain unless asked twice, which is the whole test, and so far everyone has failed it.
'What do you miss about your language?' Jokes. I'm funny in my first language, I promise. Here I'm merely pleasant, which is worse than it sounds.
'What did your father teach you without meaning to?' How to leave a place better than you found it. He did it with campsites; I try it with people.
'What is it actually like being sixteen right now?' Adults only tell me what it was like for them. I keep a whole speech ready and it goes stale weekly.
'What's your favorite sound?' Rain on a tin roof, then my grandfather clearing his throat before a story. Nobody asks about sounds. They should.
'What would you do with a free Tuesday?' Not a weekend, a Tuesday. The answer reveals everything. Mine: the sea, alone, with bread for the gulls.
